pos: n. (the act of regaining what was lost, or restoration from sickness or from a judgment)
etymology: From Latin recuperare, to get again, through French recovrer. Webster keeps the plain sense: to regain a thing, a health, or a right taken in court.
biblical_def:
Scripture's word for this work is restore, not a program. The LORD restoreth the soul and leads it in paths of righteousness for His name's sake. He promises to restore the years the locust hath eaten. The spiritual are told to restore a brother overtaken in a fault, in the spirit of meekness. The father of the prodigal does not manage a process. He receives a son who was lost and is found.

Recovery, then, is God's act of giving back what sin, judgment, or the curse took. It is not a mood and not a brand. A man may regain goods, health, or a brother's place in the church. The ground of every true recovery is the name of the LORD, not the skill of the one who lost the thing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the act of regaining, retaking, or obtaining possession of anything lost; restoration from sickness; the obtaining of a right by verdict and judgment.
webster_full: RECOVERY, n. The act of regaining, retaking or obtaining possession of anything lost.
Restoration from sickness or apparent death.
The obtaining of right to something by a verdict and judgment of court from an opposing party in a suit.
scriptures: He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake.
And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you.
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to be merry.
corruption_summary: The age renamed restoration as a lifestyle brand, so that recovery means a managed identity rather than God giving back what was lost.
corruption_paragraphs: The plain word still means to get something back. The corruption is the transfer of the work from God to a program. A man is taught to say he is in recovery as a permanent name, rather than to confess the fault, receive restoration, and walk again in righteousness.

Scripture does not deny the slowness of a body coming back from sickness. Webster already names that sense. What it will not allow is a recovery that never returns the man to the paths of righteousness, or a church that manages the fallen brother instead of restoring him.
roots_summary: Hebrew shub (H7725), to turn back, restore; Greek katartizo (G2675), to mend, restore to a former condition.
roots_lines: Psalm 23:3 uses the restoring work of the Shepherd. The soul is brought back, and the path is righteousness, not a private feeling.
Galatians 6:1 uses katartizo, the mending of what is out of joint. The spiritual man restores. He does not display the fault.
usage: He restoreth my soul — recovery that begins and ends with the Shepherd's name.
Restore such an one — the church's duty toward a brother overtaken, not a public process.

pos: n. (an author's sole right in his own original literary work)
etymology: English compound of copy and right. Webster defines it as the sole right an author has in his own original literary compositions, including the right to print, publish, and vend them, and the same right in an assignee.
biblical_def:
Scripture does not use the modern legal term, but it does forbid theft and it does require that a laborer receive what is due. Thou shalt not steal. The Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel. Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it.

Copyright is the civil form of that duty applied to an author's words. To take a man's book, print it, and sell it as if the labor were yours is theft wearing a press. The right is not a claim to own truth. Truth is God's. The right is a claim against another man who would vend your labor without leave.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the sole right which an author has in his own original literary compositions; the exclusive right to print, publish, and vend them, for his own benefit, or the same right in an assignee.
webster_full: COPYRIGHT, n. The sole right which an author has in his own original literary compositions.
The exclusive right of an author to print, publish and vend his own literary works, for his own benefit.
The like right in the hands of an assignee.
scriptures: Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel.
Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn.
Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it.
corruption_summary: The age treats another man's sentences as free raw material, as if labor ceases to be property once it can be copied.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is not the existence of a civil right. Webster already names the author's sole right to print and vend his own work. The corruption is the habit of taking that work, altering a line, and publishing it as one's own, then calling the theft sharing.
Scripture does not make an author the owner of God's truth. It does make him the owner of his labor. To muzzle the ox is the same sin whether the ox treads corn or the scribe spends a year on a book.
roots_summary: No biblical headword. The moral ground is theft (Exo 20:15) and the laborer's due (Deu 25:4; 1Co 9:14).
roots_lines: The eighth commandment covers goods taken without right. A copied book is still goods.
Paul's ox is the working minister. The same justice covers the working author.
usage: Thou shalt not steal — the commandment under every unauthorized reprint.
Withhold not good from them to whom it is due — the author's labor is due its hire.

pos: n. (self-murder; the designed destruction of one's own life)
etymology: Latin suicidium, from sui, of oneself, and caedere, to slay. Webster: self-murder; the act of designedly destroying one's own life. To constitute the crime, he adds, the person must be of years of discretion and of sound mind.
biblical_def:
The sixth commandment is Thou shalt not kill. The body of a believer is not his to dispose of. Know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost, and ye are not your own? Ye are bought with a price. The jailer at Philippi drew his sword against himself when he supposed the prisoners fled. Paul's word stopped him. Saul fell upon his own sword rather than be abused by the uncircumcised, and the text records the act as the end of a rejected king, not as a permitted exit.

Suicide is self-murder. It is the taking of a life God gave and, for the saint, a life God bought. Despair is real. Affliction is real. Neither transfers ownership of the body from God to the sufferer.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): self-murder; the act of designedly destroying one's own life. The person must be of years of discretion and of sound mind. Also, one guilty of self-murder.
webster_full: SUICIDE, n. Self-murder; the act of designedly destroying one's own life.
To constitute suicide the person must be of years of discretion and of sound mind.
One guilty of self-murder; a felo de se.
scriptures: What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own?
For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.
And the keeper of the prison awaking out of his sleep, and seeing the prison doors open, he drew out his sword, and would have killed himself, supposing that the prisoners had been fled.
corruption_summary: The age renamed self-murder as a private right, as if a man owned the life God gave and Christ bought.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption does not deny that men despair. It denies the Owner. A culture that calls self-murder autonomy has already rejected the sixth commandment and the purchase price of the body.

Webster's limit still matters. He requires years of discretion and a sound mind before the civil crime is complete. That limit is mercy in a court. It is not permission. The body remains God's whether the mind is clear or clouded. The church's answer to the despairing is the gospel and the stay of a brother's hand, as Paul stayed the jailer's, not a new name for the sin.
roots_summary: No single biblical headword. The act is judged under murder (Exo 20:13) and under the purchase of the body (1Co 6:19-20).
roots_lines: Latin suicidium says plainly what the euphemism hides: the slaying of oneself.
Acts 16:28 is the apostolic interruption of the act. The text does not admire the sword. It stops it.
usage: Ye are not your own — the sentence that ends every claim of a private right to self-murder.
The jailer would have killed himself — recorded so the church would know the word that stops the hand.

pos: n. (the state of a trader unable to pay his debts, or the act of becoming so)
etymology: From bankrupt, likely bank-broken, the fund broken, with Latin ruptus, broken. Webster confines the strict legal term to traders. Other men, he says, are insolvent. The state is inability to pay all debts.
biblical_def:
Scripture does not know the statute, but it knows the debtor who cannot pay and the wicked man who borrows and pays not again. The righteous sheweth mercy and giveth. Owe no man any thing, but to love one another. The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender. In the parable, the servant who had not to pay was commanded to be sold, and payment to be made — until the lord forgave the debt.

Bankruptcy is the civil name for a broken fund. It may be the fruit of fraud, of folly, or of a providence that emptied the barn. The moral question is not the statute. It is whether the man pays what he can, tells the truth about what he cannot, and refuses to treat unpaid debt as a clever escape.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the state of being a bankrupt, or insolvent; inability to pay all debts. Also the act of becoming a bankrupt, as by absconding or by failure in trade.
webster_full: BANKRUPTCY, n. The state of being a bankrupt, or insolvent; inability to pay all debts.
The act of becoming a bankrupt; the act of rendering one's self a bankrupt, as by absconding, or otherwise; failure in trade.
scriptures: The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again: but the righteous sheweth mercy, and giveth.
Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law.
The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender.
But forasmuch as he had not to pay, his lord commanded him to be sold, and his wife, and children, and all that he had, and payment to be made.
corruption_summary: The age treats a broken fund as a strategy, so that unpaid debts become a clever reset rather than a debt still owed in the sight of God.
corruption_paragraphs: A statute may discharge a man from a civil collection. It cannot make Psalm 37:21 untrue. The wicked borroweth and payeth not again. A righteous man who cannot pay tells the truth, pays what the hand can pay, and does not abscond.

Webster already separates the trader's bankruptcy from a general insolvency, and he names absconding as one way a man renders himself a bankrupt. Hiding the goods is not the same act as an empty barn. The corruption collapses both into a lifestyle.
roots_summary: No biblical statute-word. The moral field is debt, the borrower as servant (Pro 22:7), and the wicked who pays not again (Psa 37:21).
roots_lines: Latin ruptus is the break. The fund is broken. The duty to the creditor is not.
Matthew 18 sets the unpayable debt under a lord who can forgive. Forgiveness is his act, not the debtor's trick.
usage: The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again — the verse a discharge paper does not repeal.
The borrower is servant to the lender — why a broken fund is never a small thing.

pos: n. (error; a blunder of sense or imagination; a vision that is not from the mouth of the LORD)
etymology: Latin hallucinatio, from hallucinor, to blunder, to wander in mind. Webster's first sense is simply error, blunder, mistake. His medical sense is a faulty sense or an erroneous imagination.
biblical_def:
Scripture names the thing without the Latin. God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie. The false prophets speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD. In the latter times some shall give heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils.

A hallucination is a sight or a sentence that presents itself as real and is not. In the body, the sense misfires. In the church, a man reports a vision his own heart produced and calls it the LORD. The test is not how vivid the picture is. The test is whether it came out of the mouth of the LORD.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): error; blunder; mistake. In medicine, faulty sense or erroneous imagination, sometimes a symptom of disease.
webster_full: HALLUCINATION, n. Error; blunder; mistake.
In medicine, faulty sense or erroneous imagination.
Hallucinations of the senses arise from some defect in the organs of sense, or from some unusual circumstances attending the object, and are sometimes symptoms of general disease.
scriptures: And for this cause God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie:
Thus saith the LORD of hosts, Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you: they make you vain: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD.
Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils;
corruption_summary: The age uses the word to dismiss every unwelcome sight as a private misfire, and also to baptize a machine's invented sentence as if error were insight.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions travel under one noun. The first treats Jeremiah's test as cruelty. A vision of one's own heart is still called a word from God if the speaker feels it strongly. The second treats a fabricated sentence, whether from a fevered sense or from a tool, as close enough to truth.

Webster's medical sense is honest. A sick eye can misreport a room. That fact does not make the false prophet's vision a medical event, and it does not make a lie into a revelation. Strong delusion is judicial. A vision of one's own heart is theft of the LORD's mouth.
roots_summary: Latin hallucinor, to blunder. The biblical counterparts are delusion (2Th 2:11) and a vision of one's own heart (Jer 23:16).
roots_lines: The Latin root is a blunder, not a revelation. That order must be kept.
Jeremiah 23:16 is the test the age refuses: not out of the mouth of the LORD.
usage: They speak a vision of their own heart — hallucination wearing a prophet's cloak.
Strong delusion, that they should believe a lie — error sent as judgment, not as insight.

pos: n. (the fraudulent taking, for one's own use, of money or goods entrusted to one's care)
etymology: English, from an older verb meaning to make away with by fraud. Webster: the act of fraudulently appropriating to one's own use the money or goods entrusted to one's care and management. Also, the thing appropriated.
biblical_def:
Paul's word to servants is not purloining, but shewing all good fidelity. The unjust steward was accused of wasting his lord's goods. Ananias kept back part of the price, his wife being privy to it, and laid the rest at the apostles' feet as if it were the whole.

Embezzlement is theft inside a trust. The goods were lawfully in the man's hands. The sin is the turning of that custody into ownership. A steward, a treasurer, a servant, a public officer — the office does not soften the act. It aggravates it, because fidelity was the office.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the act of fraudulently appropriating to one's own use the money or goods entrusted to one's care and management. Also, the thing appropriated.
webster_full: EMBEZZLEMENT, n. The act of fraudulently appropriating to one's own use, the money or goods entrusted to one's care and management.
The thing appropriated.
scriptures: Not purloining, but shewing all good fidelity; that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things.
And he said also unto his disciples, There was a certain rich man, which had a steward; and the same was accused unto him that he had wasted his goods.
And kept back part of the price, his wife also being privy to it, and brought a certain part, and laid it at the apostles' feet.
corruption_summary: The age calls a trusted theft a discrepancy, so that a steward can waste his lord's goods and keep the name of manager.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is verbal. Purloining becomes shrinkage. Keeping back part of the price becomes a reporting error. The goods were entrusted. The hand that keeps them has already judged itself.

Ananias did not steal from a stranger's house. He kept back what he had placed, by his own mouth, under the apostles. Embezzlement is often exactly that: a man using the cover of a true gift, a true office, or a true account to retain what is no longer his.
roots_summary: Greek nosphizo (G3557), to set apart for oneself, keep back, as Ananias did; apostereo, to defraud, stands near the same field.
roots_lines: Titus 2:10 forbids purloining in the very sentence that tells servants to adorn the doctrine.
Acts 5:2 is the church's exhibit. The lie and the kept-back price are one act.
usage: Not purloining, but shewing all good fidelity — the servant's rule, and the treasurer's.
Kept back part of the price — embezzlement that still looks like a gift.

pos: n. (the crime of counterfeiting a writing, a name, or a coin; also the false thing itself)
etymology: From forge, originally to work metal into shape. Webster notes that sense as rare. The living sense is the crime of counterfeiting: a writing, a name, a note, or a coin, to the prejudice of another. Also the counterfeit thing itself.
biblical_def:
How do ye say, We are wise, and the law of the LORD is with us? Lo, certainly in vain made he it; the pen of the scribes is in vain. Paul warns the Thessalonians not to be shaken by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter as from us. John closes the book with a testimony against any man who adds to the words of the prophecy.

Forgery is a false making offered as a true one. A counterfeit coin, a false name on a bond, a letter that pretends to be Paul's, a pen that pretends to be the law of the LORD — the instrument changes. The sin is the same. Something is made to pass for what it is not, and another man bears the loss.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the crime of counterfeiting, as of coin, notes, or a bond; also the counterfeit thing itself. Forgery may consist in counterfeiting a writing, or in setting a false name to it.
webster_full: FORGERY, n. The crime of counterfeiting; as the forgery of coin, or of bank notes, or of a bond.
Forgery may consist in counterfeiting a writing, or in setting a false name to it, to the prejudice of another person.
That which is forged or counterfeited.
scriptures: How do ye say, We are wise, and the law of the LORD is with us? Lo, certainly in vain made he it; the pen of the scribes is in vain.
That ye be not soon shaken in mind, or be troubled, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter as from us, as that the day of Christ is at hand.
For I testify unto every man that heareth the words of the prophecy of this book, If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book:
corruption_summary: The age multiplies false makings and calls them content, so that a counterfeit voice, letter, or image passes until someone else pays for it.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster's prejudice-of-another-person is the moral core the age drops. A forged note is not a clever craft. It is a writing made to injure the man whose name or goods it counterfeits.

The same sin reaches the Scriptures when a pen pretends the law of the LORD is still in the hand that has already made the pen vain. Adding to the prophecy is not editing. It is forgery against the Author.
roots_summary: No single biblical headword. The field is a vain pen (Jer 8:8), a letter as from us (2Th 2:2), and adding to the prophecy (Rev 22:18).
roots_lines: The old sense, working metal, is why the word still sounds like a shop. The crime is a shop that stamps a false name.
Second Thessalonians 2:2 assumes forgeries of Paul were already in circulation. The church was told not to be shaken by them.
usage: Nor by letter as from us — a forged apostolic hand.
The pen of the scribes is in vain — a forgery that still quotes the law.

pos: n. (one who respects; in Scripture, one who judges by outward circumstance)
etymology: English agent-noun from respect. Webster says it is chiefly used in the phrase respecter of persons: one who regards the external circumstances of others in his judgment, and suffers his opinion to be biased by them, to the prejudice of candor, justice, and equity.
biblical_def:
Peter's sentence at Cornelius's house is the definition. Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons. Paul repeats the doctrine as law: there is no respect of persons with God. James makes the church's version a sin. If ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin, and are convinced of the law as transgressors.

A respecter is not a man who honors whom honor is due. He is a judge whose eye has left the case and settled on the coat, the purse, the tribe, or the chair. God does not judge that way. A church that does has already left the gospel Peter preached to a Gentile.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one that respects; chiefly in respecter of persons, one who regards the external circumstances of others in his judgment, to the prejudice of candor, justice, and equity.
webster_full: RESPECTER, n. One that respects; chiefly used in the phrase, respecter of persons.
A person who regards the external circumstances of others in his judgment, and suffers his opinion to be biased by them, to the prejudice of candor, justice and equity.
scriptures: Then Peter opened his mouth, and said, Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons:
For there is no respect of persons with God.
But if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin, and are convinced of the law as transgressors.
corruption_summary: The age either flatters the powerful without naming the sin, or pretends justice means ignoring every real difference God Himself named.
corruption_paragraphs: James does not forbid a judge to see that one man is rich and another poor. He forbids the judgment that follows the gold ring and despises the poor man. That is respect of persons. It is sin.

The other corruption swings the phrase into a denial of every distinction Scripture draws — male and female, ruler and subject, parent and child. God is no respecter of persons. He is not thereby no maker of persons. Peter learned that a Gentile may hear the gospel. He did not learn that God has no offices.
roots_summary: Greek prosopolemptes (G4381), one who takes the face, who accepts a person by outward appearance. Acts 10:34.
roots_lines: The Greek is face-taking. The judge receives the face and loses the case.
Romans 2:11 sets the same phrase over Jew and Gentile. The gospel does not bend to the face.
usage: God is no respecter of persons — Peter's door into the Gentile house.
If ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin — James's charge against a gold-ring church.
